study.title: A blueprint for <i>Vibrio</i> surveillance and risk reduction in Europe

cover.headline: **Europe needs a Vibrio surveillance system** before climate change turns coastal waters into infection hotspots

slides.title: Rising sea temperatures are pushing tropical bacteria into European coastlines with no coordinated tracking system.
slides.body:
Vibrio bacteria cause wound and foodborne infections. They used to stay in tropical waters. Warming seas are bringing them north.

Recent outbreaks in the Baltic and North Seas show Europe is unprepared. Surveillance is patchy and public warnings are limited.

slides.title: Vibrio infections are increasing in frequency and moving to higher latitudes as extreme weather reshapes coastal waters.
slides.body:
Vibrio vulnificus and V. parahaemolyticus now appear in regions that were previously too cold. Climate change is expanding suitable habitat for these pathogens.

Europe needs integrated monitoring that combines environmental tracking, genomic surveillance, and public health communication.

slides.title: Vibrio species thrive in warm seawater and infect people through open wounds or contaminated shellfish.
slides.body:
The bacteria are recognized as a sentinel of climate-linked infectious disease. But no unified European framework exists to monitor outbreaks or warn the public.

Coordinated preparedness will protect health systems and coastal communities as waters continue warming.

caveats: This is a policy and surveillance blueprint, not a study measuring new clinical or environmental data.
The abstract does not quantify infection rates, outbreak frequency, or the geographic spread with specific numbers or trends.

source.abstract: Vibrio bacteria, long regarded as pathogens of tropical waters, are now emerging across numerous European coastlines as rising sea surface temperatures and extreme weather reshape microbial ecologies. Wound and foodborne infections caused by Vibrio vulnificus , Vibrio parahaemolyticus and other non-cholera species are increasing in frequency and latitude. Recent heat-related outbreaks in the Baltic and North Seas demonstrate that climate change is already expanding the suitable habitat for these bacteria. Yet across Europe surveillance remains patchy, diagnostics inconsistent, and risk communication limited. Europe requires an integrated approach to Vibrio preparedness, uniting environmental monitoring, genomic epidemiology surveillance, and public health awareness. Recognising Vibrio spp. as a sentinel of climate-linked infectious disease will be necessary for protecting coastal communities, seafood safety, and health systems in a warming world.
